extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of Renaissance humanism, literary historians, and readers of Erasmus' biography
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and historical-literary analysis of Erasmus' life, writings (notably The Praise of Folly), and contemporary practices (preaching, patronage, university offices) as described in a scholarly biography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid scholastic pedantry in preaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of scholastic preaching that displays 'uncommon learning' by teasing theological meaning out of letters, syllables, and grammatical agreements (e.g., attempts to express the mystery of the Trinity in the rudiments of grammar).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage gives concrete anti-examples: a preacher who 'showed as plainly as any mathematician' that the Trinity is expressed in grammar and another who deduces theological mysteries by splitting the letters of 'Jesus'. These are presented as misguided exhibitionism—preaching should avoid abstruse grammatical curiosities and focus on intelligible, substantive theological teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not misapply rhetorical principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning against 'misapplying and exaggerating the good principles of rhetoric'—friars and others adopting rhetorical forms in a distorted, theatrical way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misapplied rhetoric produces theatrical decorations, empty show, and substitutes outward pomp (ceremonies, titles, blessings) for real spiritual duties. Effective rhetoric should serve clarity and moral purpose, not self-display or hollow ceremony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical conduct should emulate Christ (poverty, teaching, prayer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Normative claim (through Folly's ironic speech) that if popes and clerics truly imitated Christ's poverty, toil, teaching, cross, and scorn of this world they would lose worldly wealth and honours but gain vigils, prayers, study, and the painful toils of true Christian life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list of what would be lost (wealth, honours, dispensations, indulgences, etc.) and what would be gained (vigils, prayers, fasts, sermons, study) serves as an implicit standard for evaluating clerical virtue: prioritize spiritual duties over worldly comforts and showmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper scriptural interpretation; avoid readings that justify violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of theologians who misread texts (example: misinterpretation of 'hereticum hominem post unam et alteram correptionem devita' as mandating killing heretics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive rigor is required; Scripture should not be twisted to justify violent or intolerant practices. The preferred approach is persuasion and argument ('convincing them by argument') rather than coercion or execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lightness/flippancy as a rhetorical device responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus' defence that the 'flippancy' in the Moria (Praise of Folly) is only apparent—a lightness of touch intended to commend a serious underlying purpose, not to launch personal attacks or promote indecency or sedition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire and humour can be legitimate critical tools when they illuminate serious faults; however, the writer should avoid indecent or seditious content and should not aim at gratuitous personal abuse or at needlessly provoking hostility against valuable institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of the Lady Margaret Reader of Divinity (formal expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative/academic requirements for the Lady Margaret readership: the reader 'must read libere, sollenniter, and aperte'; read every accustomed day in each term and during the long vacation up to September 8 (may cease in Lent if chancellor thinks fit); no fees beyond salary; must read such works in divinity as the chancellor with the college of doctors judges necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This office was intended to be no sinecure: the reader must devote himself wholly to regular public reading/lectures in divinity, adhere to the specified schedule, and accept the salary (here noted as sixty-five dollars a year) as the sole remuneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtly tactics for gaining favour and patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical advice for advancement at court: 'give your forehead such a rubbing that you will never blush at anything; mix yourself in everybody's business; elbow aside everyone you can; give nothing without hope of a return; agree to all things with all men.' Also: exploit jealousy by 'riding two horses at once', hire suitors, threaten to leave to increase your value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are explicit, somewhat cynical strategies for securing patronage: be shamelessly sociable, prioritize self-advantage, cultivate multiple patrons, and use absence/threatened departure to sharpen patrons' desire. Presented as tactical (and morally ambiguous) recommendations based on lived practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting benefices/pensions: moral and practical considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of the common practice of resigning a living with duties in exchange for a life-pension without duties, and Warham's reluctant exception in Erasmus' case (justified by Erasmus' rare learning and devotion to literary studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This material sets out an evaluative tension: accepting a benefice without performing its pastoral duties may be seen as an abuse of trust, but exceptions are sometimes made for exceptional scholars if the patron judges the broader public benefit (scholarship) justifies it. It serves as guidance for assessing the moral legitimacy of such arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations about teaching vs. scholarly work
rubrics_metrics.description: Implied criterion that holders of academic offices (e.g., the Lady Margaret readership) are expected to fulfil specified teaching/reading duties (focused on divinity), not to substitute other scholarly pursuits (e.g., teaching Greek) or neglect teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account implies negative assessment where holders (like Erasmus) neglect formal duties: being an accomplished scholar does not excuse failure to meet institutional teaching obligations; institutions expect regular public instruction as specified by statutes.
